speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you are experiencing progressive swelling and pain in your right ring finger; can you tell me exactly when these symptoms started and if they are constant or come and go? Additionally, does the swelling extend to other fingers or joints, or is it isolated to this digit?

speaker: Patient
text: 22-year-old male. The patient reports that the pain and swelling in his right ring finger began 2 days ago while playing football. He recalls his finger got caught in the jersey of another player, who then pulled away forcefully.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details; the mechanism of injury involving a forceful pull while playing football is very specific. Did you hear or feel a distinct "pop" at the time of the injury, and can you still extend or flex that finger fully?

REQUEST IMAGES: X-ray Right hand (AP/Lateral), Ultrasound Right ring finger.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Progressive swelling and pain in the right ring finger. I also have Inability to flex the right ring finger at the distal interphalangeal joint when making a fist, Pain at the distal interphalangeal joint, Extended right ring finger in resting position.

speaker: Doctor
text: That combination of symptoms—specifically the inability to flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint while the finger remains extended in the resting position—is highly characteristic of a mallet finger injury. Given the mechanism of a direct pull on the finger, have you noticed any bruising or deformity at the tip of the finger? Please also confirm if you have a recent X-ray showing avulsion or subluxation of the distal phalanx.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant medical history. Social history: Student and active in sports, particularly football. Non-smoker and drinks alcohol socially.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Mallet Finger (Extensor tendon avulsion or rupture at the distal phalanx).

The clinical picture of an extended resting position, inability to actively flex the DIP joint, and a mechanism of forced flexion following a direct pull is pathognomonic for this injury. The patient's young age and active lifestyle are consistent with this traumatic etiology, and the lack of significant past medical history supports an acute isolated injury rather than an inflammatory or systemic cause.

DIAGNOSIS_READY_Answer: Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion
